1.note: The author is using the phrase **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
To translate this expression here and in the rest of this chapter, see how you translated the same expression in 18:11. Alternate translation: [the Ammonites]

2.note: In this instance, the author is using the term **said** to introduce what David was thinking or saying to himself. David did not necessarily say this out loud to anyone. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing what people say to themselves or think. Alternate translation: [And David said to himself] or [And David thought]

2.q: אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־חֶ֣סֶד ׀ עִם־חָנ֣וּן בֶּן־נָחָ֗שׁ כִּֽי־עָשָׂ֨ה אָבִ֤י⁠ו עִמִּ⁠י֙ חֶ֔סֶד
2.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since his father did kindness with me, I will do kindness with Hanun, the son of Nahash]

3.q: הַֽ⁠מְכַבֵּ֨ד דָּוִ֤יד אֶת־אָבִ֨י⁠ךָ֙ בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֔י⁠ךָ כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֥ח לְ⁠ךָ֖ מְנַחֲמִ֑ים
3.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [In your eyes, since David has sent consolers to you, is he honoring your father]

3.q: הַֽ⁠מְכַבֵּ֨ד דָּוִ֤יד אֶת־אָבִ֨י⁠ךָ֙ בְּ⁠עֵינֶ֔י⁠ךָ כִּֽי־שָׁלַ֥ח לְ⁠ךָ֖ מְנַחֲמִ֑ים
3.note: The commanders are using the question form to deny emphatically that David was honoring Hanun’s father. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not believe that David is honoring your father by sending consolers to you!]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:3. Alternate translation: [In your view] or [In your judgment]

3.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֡א בַּ֠⁠עֲבוּר לַ⁠חְקֹ֨ר וְ⁠לַ⁠הֲפֹ֤ךְ וּ⁠לְ⁠רַגֵּל֙ הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ בָּ֥אוּ עֲבָדָ֖י⁠ו אֵלֶֽי⁠ךָ
3.note: The commanders are using the question form to strongly assert that David’s servants have come for a different reason, to explore, overthrow, and spy on the land. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No, David’s servants have come to you in order to explore and to overthrow and to spy on the land!]

The commanders are describing one potential event, that David and his army might **overthrow** the **land**, before describing another event that would precede it, that his **servants** would **explore** and **spy on** it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they would happen. Alternate translation: [in order to explore and to spy on the land so that David can overthrow it]

The terms **explore** and **spy on the land** mean similar things. The commanders are using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to investigate the land thoroughly so that David can overthrow it]

The commanders is speaking as if David would actually **overthrow** the **land**, or turn it upside down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to conquer]

4.note: Shaving the men and cutting their garments in the middle was a symbolic action by which the Ammonite king sought to humiliate David’s messengers. (See the further discussion in the Introduction to this chapter.) If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he humiliated them by shaving them and cutting their garments in the middle, to their buttocks]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **he shaved them**, he means that Hanun had his servants shave off the beards of David’s servants. The author indicates that explicitly in the next verse. (The parallel passage in 2 Samuel 10:4 indicates that he had them shave off half of their beards. See the discussion in the introduction to this chapter of that action.) You could indicate the meaning of this expression explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he shaved off their beards] or [and he shaved off half of their beards]

5.note: Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And someone declared to David] or [And David was told]

5.q: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֣ח לִ⁠קְרָאתָ֔⁠ם כִּי־הָי֥וּ הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֖ים נִכְלָמִ֣ים מְאֹ֑ד
5.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [and because the men were greatly humiliated, he sent to meet them]
Since the author indicates later in this verse the purpose for which David **sent** messengers **to meet** these men, you do not need to explain that purpose here.

The expression **were greatly humiliated** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [this had greatly humiliated the men]

The author is saying **the king** to mean his messengers, who were speaking on his behalf. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the king’s messengers told them]

6.note: The author is speaking as if the Ammonites had made themselves smell so bad that they were offensive to David. He is using this image to mean that the Ammonites had provoked David. Your language may have a comparable image that you could use in your translation. You could also use plain language. If you have already translated the books of 1 Samuel and 2 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 13:4 and in the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 10:6. Alternate translation: [they had incensed David] or [they had provoked David]

7.note: In this context, the term **people** means “soldiers.” Alternate translation: [and his soldiers]
The pronoun **they** refers to the many soldiers whom the Ammonites had hired. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the soldiers whom they had hired came]
Here, **to the face of** represents “in front of.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of]

8.note: The author adds the expression **the warriors** to clarify that by **all of the army**, he means all of the Israelite men who were regular soldiers in the army. He will describe in verse 17 how David later mobilized “all of Israel,” that is, all the Israelite men who were able to fight as soldiers, even if that was not what they regularly did. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the whole regular army]

9.note: The author is using one central location in the city wall, **the entrance** (that is, the main gate), to represent the entire wall, which served as a defensive support for the Ammonite battle line. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of the city wall]

10.note: The expression **the faces of the battle** represents the battle lines that the enemy armies had drawn up in order to fight the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [there were battle fronts ahead of him and behind him]

The term **chosen** is a verbal form that functions in this context as an adjective. The author is using it as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the chosen troops]

The expression **chosen** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the select troops] or [the elite troops]

11.note: See how you translated the term “people” in 19:7. Alternate translation: [the soldiers]

Here, **hand** represents control. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [under the control of] or [under the command of]
The pronoun **he** refers to Abishai. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Abishai arrayed them]

12.note: he pronoun **he** refers to Joab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Joab said]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [then you shall come and save me]

13.note: Here, **the cities of our God** represents the cities of Israel, where the true God was worshiped. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [our Israelite cities]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:3. Alternate translation: [as he sees fit] or [what he considers to be right]

14.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 17:8. Alternate translation: [to confront the Arameans in battle]

The author is using one part of Joab, his **face**, to represent all of him in the act of leading an attack against the Arameans. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from him as he led the attack]

15.note: The author is stating the pronoun **they** separately, ven though the verb translated as **they fled** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize that the Ammonites independently took the same action as the Arameans. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [and for their part, they also fled]
See how you translated the similar expression in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [from Abishai his brother as he led the attack against them]

16.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 17:21. Alternate translation: [they had been defeated as they opposed Israel in battle]

The expression **had been defeated** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Israelites had defeated them as they opposed them in battle]

The author is referring to the Euphrates River, which was the most important river in this region and so was sometimes simply called **the River**. You could use your language’s name for this river if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar expression in 18:3. Alternate translation: [the Euphrates River] or [the River of Perath]

**Shophach** is a variant spelling of the name “Shobach,” which occurs in the parallel passage in 2 Samuel 10:18. Recall whether your translation team decided to use the same name for a given person in each instance where it appears or whether you decided to use the name that the biblical author does, even if that is a variant. Alternate translation: [Joram]

This expression depicts Shophach as being in front of this combined army, and the author is using that position to represent his leadership of the army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [was leading them] or [was commanding them]

17.note: The expression **it was declared to David** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And someone told David about this]

The author is using the name **Israel** to represent the soldiers of the Israelite army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the whole Israelite army]

18.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 19:14. Alternate translation: [from the Israelites as they attacked]

The author is using one person who was involved in this action of the Israelite army, **David**, to represent the entire army. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and David’s soldiers killed … And David’s soldiers killed Shophach]

19.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:46. Alternate translation: [they had been defeated to the face of Israel]
See how you translated the expression “to the face of Israel” in 19:16. Alternate translation: [they had been defeated as they opposed Israel in battle]

The expression **had been struck** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Israelites had defeated them as they opposed them in battle]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they asked to have peaceful relations with David]
